parsed_answer.content: When designing high-throughput, low-latency microservices architectures, choosing the right inter-process communication protocol is critical. Traditional REST APIs, predominantly built on HTTP/1.1 and JSON, suffer from severe performance bottlenecks due to text-based payload serialization, head-of-line blocking, and redundant metadata transmission over multiple discrete TCP connections. In contrast, gRPC—an open-source remote procedure call framework initially developed by Google—leverages HTTP/2 transport and Protocol Buffers (protobuf) to achieve dramatically higher throughput, smaller wire sizes, and lower CPU overhead. By compiling schema definitions into strongly typed binary stubs across multiple languages, gRPC eliminates runtime schema parsing overhead, optimizes network utilization via multiplexing, and natively supports bidirectional streaming out of the box.

rows: HTTP/1.1 (often new TCP handshake per request)
Native unary, client, server, and bidirectional streams

items: Protocol Buffers serialize data into dense binary formats using tag-length-value (TLV) encodings, skipping field names entirely on the wire and storing only numeric field tags and encoded values.
HTTP/2 multiplexing allows multiple concurrent request-response streams to travel over a single TCP connection, completely eliminating HTTP/1.1 head-of-line blocking.
HPACK header compression drastically reduces network overhead by tracking previously sent headers in a shared dynamic state table and referencing them via indexing.
Code generation yields highly optimized, zero-reflection marshalling routines that bypass the heavy runtime metadata introspection required by Jackson or Gson in JSON-based REST frameworks.

parsed_answer.content: Senior production gotcha: While gRPC significantly outperforms REST for internal microservice communication, it is rarely a drop-in replacement for public-facing web applications. Standard browsers do not currently expose the low-level HTTP/2 framing required to invoke gRPC channels directly without an intermediary proxy like Envoy running gRPC-Web. Furthermore, debugging gRPC payloads requires specialized tooling (such as grpcurl or BloomRPC) because binary protobuf data is entirely unreadable in standard network inspection tabs.
